unit.title: Water — The Essence of Life
unit.aboutUnit: Highlights the crucial role of nature as a home to animals, birds, and plants, with water being the primary sustainer of all terrestrial and aquatic life. Emphasizes environmental observation, states of matter, the water cycle, and responsible water conservation.

chapter.title: Water — The Essence of Life
chapter.tagline: Discover the incredible journey of water across solid, liquid, and vapour forms, uncover Earth’s hidden freshwater sources, and explore pond ecosystems.
chapter.overview: Introduces states of water, the water cycle, groundwater seepage, surface vs underground water, aquatic adaptations, and water conservation ethics.

characters.name: Jyoti
characters.bio: Asks thought-provoking questions about where rain comes from and how water changes forms.

sections.title: Rain at the Window — Where Does Water Come From?
sections.subtitle: Discovering Earth's water distribution and freshwater scarcity

storyNarrative.setting: Inside home during a monsoon downpour, watching raindrops race down window panes.
storyNarrative.dialogue: “It is raining! Afreen rushed to the window where Jyoti was watching tiny raindrops slide down the glass. ‘Where do you think all this water comes from, and where does it go after it hits the ground?’ asked Afreen.”
storyNarrative.audioText: Afreen and Jyoti watch rain droplets slide down the glass and ask about water sources.

sections.textbookCoreText: It is raining. Afreen rushed to the window where Jyoti was already watching tiny raindrops slide down the glass. “Where do you think all this water comes from, and where does it go?” asked Afreen. Although most of Earth’s surface is covered with water, the majority of it is salty, leaving less than 3% as freshwater.

concept.heading: Earth's Water Distribution (Salty vs Freshwater)
concept.explanation: Around 71% of Earth is covered in water. But over 97% is salty ocean water. Less than 3% is freshwater, and most of that is locked in polar ice caps and high mountain glaciers. Only a tiny fraction is accessible in lakes, rivers, and groundwater.
concept.keyRule: Over 97% of Earth's water is salty ocean water; less than 3% is freshwater.

content.speaker: Afreen & Jyoti
content.dialogue: “Where do you think all this water comes from, and where does it go?”

content.text: Wular Lake in Jammu and Kashmir is one of the largest freshwater lakes in Asia. It acts as a giant natural flood basin and sustains hundreds of bird species.

blocks.title: Interactive Lab: Global Blue Planet 3D Water & Land Ratio Explorer

content.interactiveTitle: Global Blue Planet 3D Water & Land Ratio Explorer
content.pedagogicalObjective: Understand that water covers over 70% of Earth's surface and is essential for all living organisms.
content.explanation: Afreen and Jyoti watch raindrops on their window and wonder how much of Earth is covered by water. Students rotate a 3D Earth globe, toggle ocean and land layers, and discover that over 71% of Earth's surface is blue water.
content.simpleExplanation: Spin planet Earth in 3D to see why our home is called the Blue Planet, covered in 71% shimmering oceans!
content.stemExplanation: Planetary hydrology and geosphere surface area distribution (361 million km² water vs 149 million km² land).

questions.prompt: Why can humans not drink ocean water directly?
questions.hint: Think about what gives seawater its salty taste.
questions.explanation: Ocean water has around 35 grams of dissolved salt per litre, which dehydrates the human body.

sections.title: Three Forms of Water & The Cold Glass Experiment
sections.subtitle: Observing condensation and phase changes between solid, liquid, and vapour

storyNarrative.setting: Kitchen table testing cold glasses and ice cubes.
storyNarrative.dialogue: “Jyoti asked: ‘Is there water in the air too? And is snow a form of water?’ Let's put ice in a dry steel glass and watch what happens on the outside wall!”
storyNarrative.audioText: Jyoti tests the forms of water using ice cubes.

sections.textbookCoreText: Water has different forms: liquid (rain), solid (ice, snow), and vapour (steam, humidity). Activity 2: Take a steel glass. Put some ice cubes in it. Observe small water droplets forming on the dry outer wall. Where do these droplets come from?

concept.heading: Evaporation and Condensation
concept.explanation: When water is heated by the Sun, it turns into invisible water vapour (Evaporation). When warm water vapour touches a cold surface (like the ice-cold steel glass), it cools down and turns back into liquid water droplets (Condensation).
concept.keyRule: Heating causes Evaporation (Liquid ➔ Vapour). Cooling causes Condensation (Vapour ➔ Liquid).

steps: Wipe the outside of the tumbler completely dry.
Place ice cubes inside the tumbler.
Observe water droplets condensing on the outer surface.

rows: Ice cubes turn to liquid water at room temperature
Steam rises from the pot as bubbles form
Invisible air moisture turns to liquid water droplets

blocks.title: Interactive Lab: Ice Tumbler Condensation & States of Matter Lab

content.interactiveTitle: Ice Tumbler Condensation & States of Matter Lab
content.pedagogicalObjective: Demonstrate that atmospheric water vapour condenses into liquid droplets upon touching cold surfaces.
content.explanation: Afreen places ice cubes inside a dry steel glass. Outside droplets appear. In this simulation, students adjust glass temperature from 30°C down to 0°C, watching invisible surrounding air molecules cool and condense into glittering droplets on the exterior metal surface.
content.simpleExplanation: Put ice in a dry metal glass and watch invisible water vapour in the warm air turn into glistening water beads on the outside!
content.stemExplanation: Phase transition equilibria and dew point thermodynamics: P_vapour >= P_sat(T_surface) triggering surface condensation.

questions.prompt: Where do the water droplets on the outside of an ice-cold glass come from?
options: They condensed from water vapour in the room air
questions.correctAnswer: They condensed from water vapour in the room air
questions.hint: Water cannot pass through solid steel.
questions.explanation: The invisible water vapour present in the surrounding air condenses when cooled by the glass wall.

sections.title: The Complete Water Cycle — Nature's Endless Circle
sections.subtitle: How the Sun's heat drives evaporation, clouds, rain, and snow

storyNarrative.setting: Looking at the clouds gathering over distant hills.
storyNarrative.dialogue: “The water we drink today might have fallen as rain on dinosaurs millions of years ago! It evaporates from seas, forms fluffy clouds, falls as rain, and returns to rivers in an endless dance!”
storyNarrative.audioText: Afreen explains the continuous natural water cycle.

sections.textbookCoreText: As you have seen, the Sun’s heat causes water to turn into water vapour. When this vapour rises high into the sky, it cools down and condenses into tiny drops to form clouds. When clouds become heavy, water falls back as rain, hail, or snow. This continuous cycle is called the Water Cycle.

concept.heading: Four Stages of the Water Cycle
concept.explanation:
1. Evaporation: Water from oceans, lakes, and plants heats up and rises.
2. Condensation: Vapour cools in high altitude to form clouds.
3. Precipitation: Drops merge and fall as rain or snow.
4. Collection: Water gathers in rivers, soil, and oceans.
concept.keyRule: Nature recycles 100% of Earth's water through the continuous Water Cycle.

stages.name: Evaporation
stages.desc: Sun heats ocean water turning it into vapour.

stages.name: Condensation
stages.desc: Vapour cools high up to form clouds.

stages.name: Precipitation
stages.desc: Water droplets fall as rain or snow.

stages.name: Infiltration / Seepage
stages.desc: Rainwater soaks into soil creating groundwater.

blocks.title: Interactive Lab: Thermodynamic Global Water Cycle Machine

content.pedagogicalObjective: Trace the continuous closed cycle of evaporation, condensation, precipitation, and collection.
content.explanation: Students control the global water cycle. By increasing solar heat, ocean water evaporates into vapour; cooling upper air condenses vapour into fluffy cumulus clouds; saturating clouds precipitates rain and snow over mountains, flowing back to rivers.
content.simpleExplanation: Control the Sun and weather to see how water journeys from the sea to the sky as clouds, rains down on hills, and flows right back home!
content.stemExplanation: Conservation of mass in closed thermodynamic planetary hydrologic systems (Q_solar -> latent heat of vaporization -> adiabatic cooling -> precipitation).

questions.prompt: What provides the primary energy that drives the global water cycle?
questions.hint: Think about what heats up ocean water causing it to evaporate.
questions.explanation: Solar energy warms surface water, driving evaporation into the atmosphere.

sections.title: Underground Water & The Soil Infiltration Experiment
sections.subtitle: How soil recharges aquifers and why concrete blocks rainwater

storyNarrative.setting: Garden soil patch with a clear glass and water spoon.
storyNarrative.dialogue: “When it rains on natural mud and forest soil, where does the water go? It soaks deep down! But on cemented city roads, rainwater cannot sink and runs off into drains!”
storyNarrative.audioText: Jyoti investigates soil percolation and groundwater.

sections.textbookCoreText: Activity 4: Take a transparent glass. Fill half with soil. Slowly pour water into the soil using a spoon. Observe what happens. When it rains, water sinks through soil and rocks. Water stored deep underground is called groundwater. We dig wells, tube wells, and handpumps to draw it.

concept.heading: Groundwater Recharge vs Runoff
concept.explanation: Permeable surfaces (soil, grass, forests) allow rainwater to percolate into the ground, recharging underground aquifers. Impermeable surfaces (concrete, tar roads) block infiltration, causing urban waterlogging and lowering groundwater tables.
concept.keyRule: Natural soil recharges groundwater; cemented concrete blocks recharge.

steps: Fill glass halfway with dry garden soil.
Slowly pour spoonfuls of water onto the surface.
Watch water seep through gaps between soil particles down to the base.

blocks.title: Interactive Lab: Soil Infiltration & Aquifer Percolation Tank

content.pedagogicalObjective: Observe how permeable topsoil allows rainwater percolation to recharge underground aquifers, while impermeable surfaces cause runoff.
content.explanation: Jyoti pours water on garden soil and watches it soak in, while on concrete it puddles and runs away. Students pour rain onto 3 soil columns (Garden Loam, Sand, Concrete) to observe percolation rates and well replenishment.
content.simpleExplanation: Pour water through loam soil, sand, and concrete to discover why gardens drink rainwater to fill underground wells, while concrete causes puddles and city floods!
content.stemExplanation: Darcy's Law for porous media fluid flow: Q = -K · A · (dh/dl), hydraulic conductivity and permeability coefficients across soil textures.

questions.prompt: Which surface allows the most rainwater to recharge underground aquifers?
questions.hint: Permeable earth absorbs water like a sponge.
questions.explanation: Soil has porous air pockets that allow water to filter deep underground.

interactive.pedagogicalObjective: Observe how permeable topsoil allows rainwater percolation to recharge underground aquifers, while impermeable surfaces cause runoff.

sections.title: Follow the Flow — Major Rivers of India
sections.subtitle: Mapping rivers flowing toward the Bay of Bengal vs Arabian Sea

storyNarrative.setting: Tracing a physical relief map of India with colored yarn.
storyNarrative.dialogue: “Look at India's rivers! The Ganga, Brahmaputra, Godavari, and Krishna flow east into the Bay of Bengal. But the Narmada and Tapi flow west into the Arabian Sea! Why do they flow in different directions?”
storyNarrative.audioText: Afreen traces the drainage basins of India.

sections.textbookCoreText: Activity 7: Follow the Flow! In the map, you can see rivers flowing in different directions. Some flow into the Bay of Bengal and some into the Arabian Sea. Observe the relief of the land and fill in the table.

concept.heading: Watersheds & River Drainage Basins
concept.explanation: Rivers always flow downhill from high mountains to the sea due to gravity. The peninsular plateau slopes gently from west to east, which is why most Indian rivers flow eastwards into the Bay of Bengal.
concept.keyRule: Gravity pulls water from high mountain elevations down toward sea level.

content.simpleExplanation: Explore the great rivers of India from mountain snow to ocean waves, and meet the amazing birds and fish living in peaceful wetlands!
content.stemExplanation: Topographical fluvial geomorphology, watershed catchment delineation, and Ramsar wetland ecological conservation indices.

questions.hint: It flows through a rift valley between the Vindhya and Satpura ranges.

sections.title: Life in Water — Pond Ecosystem & Aquatic Adaptations
sections.subtitle: Discovering wetland biodiversity and waterproof leaf coatings

storyNarrative.setting: Standing on a wooden footbridge over a freshwater village pond.
storyNarrative.dialogue: “Look at that lotus leaf! Water droplets sit on it like shiny silver pearls! Why don't the leaves rot underwater? Because they have a natural waxy waterproof coating!”
storyNarrative.audioText: Jyoti observes the wetland plants and animals.

sections.textbookCoreText: Afreen noticed the rain had filled up the pond. Plants and animals live together in freshwater ecosystems: dragonflies, pond herons, turtles, and water lilies. The waxy coating on lotus leaves makes them waterproof and keeps excess water from rotting the leaf.

concept.heading: Aquatic Adaptations
concept.explanation: Aquatic animals have fins, webbed feet, and gills to breathe and swim. Aquatic plants like lotus and water hyacinth have hollow spongy stems filled with air pockets to float, and waxy cuticles on leaves to repel water.
concept.keyRule: Air pockets provide buoyancy; waxy coatings repel excess water.

questions.prompt: What adaptation prevents floating lotus leaves from rotting in water?
questions.hint: Observe how water beads up on the leaf without soaking in.
questions.explanation: A hydrophobic waxy cuticle repels water droplets, keeping stomata open for photosynthesis.

sections.title: Let Us Reflect — Water Conservation & Design Thinking
sections.subtitle: Formative evaluation, matching pairs, and water-wise architecture

storyNarrative.setting: School courtyard drafting ideas for a water-conserving campus.
storyNarrative.dialogue: “What would happen if it did not rain in our region for two full years? Can we design a school building that catches every single drop of rain from its rooftop?”
storyNarrative.audioText: Afreen invites students to reflect on water conservation.

sections.textbookCoreText: Let us reflect: 1. Match the following (Ocean water, Snow, Steam, Rainwater). 2. Why can't most water on Earth be used for drinking? 3. What would happen if it did not rain for two years? 4. Can you design a house or school that conserves water wisely?

concept.heading: Rainwater Harvesting & Water Wisdom
concept.explanation: Rooftop rainwater harvesting channels rain from roofs into underground storage tanks or percolation pits, turning homes into self-sufficient water producers.
concept.keyRule: Catch water where it falls: Reduce, Reuse, Recharge.

pairs: Salty water / Not fit for drinking

questions.prompt: What would happen to your local neighborhood if it did not rain for two full years?
questions.correctAnswer: Drought, wells dry up, crops wither, drinking water shortage.
questions.hint: Think about what supplies tap water and irrigation.
questions.explanation: Without rainfall, groundwater aquifers are depleted, lakes dry up, and severe drought occurs.
